name: Ascension plan threads

card.summary: Forum posts in which a user lays out a phased list of surgeries, skincare, gym work and gear they intend to complete, posted for feedback so the plan can be refined before money and time are spent.
card.note: Plans often include surgery, prescription drugs or hormones; the posts are personal plans, not medical advice.

quick.overview:
An ascension plan thread is a post on a looksmaxxing forum in which a member sets out, in order, what they intend to do to improve their appearance: skincare, body-fat and gym goals, hair, height work, dental or facial surgery, and the dates they hope to do them. It is posted so that other members can comment before the member commits.

The appeal is organisation. Putting the sequence, timing and budget in writing turns a vague wish to look better into phases with milestones, and the replies act as a free second opinion. Threads vary from a few lines to multi-phase documents with photos, "failos" (perceived flaws) and target dates.
quick.how: Posters usually start with photos and a list of perceived weak points, then split the plan into phases by year or by goal, for example skin and leanness first, then orthodontics or jaw surgery, then smaller procedures. Replies typically suggest reordering steps, ask for before-and-after photos later, or comment on feasibility and budget.
quick.risks: The plans are written by individuals, often teenagers or young adults, and some include major surgery or prescription hormones. Replies come from anonymous peers rather than clinicians, and tone can be harsh. Surgeons and orthodontists, not forum replies, determine what a given face and bite actually call for.

lead: An ascension plan thread is a type of post on looksmaxxing forums such as looksmax.org in which a member publishes a staged plan for improving their appearance ("ascending") and asks the community for feedback. A typical plan lists current photos, the features the poster wants to change, and an ordered set of steps with target dates.[1][2]

Plans commonly combine several areas of looksmaxxing: skin treatment (one poster mentions finishing a tretinoin course), body-fat targets and gym frequency, height work, and orthodontic or jaw surgery planned for an age when the poster can afford it or has finished growing.[1][2][3] Posters often organise this into numbered phases with dates, such as a "Phase 1" for height and facial skeleton in the second half of a year.[2]

The format works as a public planning document: writing out the order of steps and the budget lets other members point out gaps, and some repliers ask the poster to share progress photos later.[2] Orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery, which features in several plans, is typically planned by a surgeon and orthodontist together, often with 3D simulations, and has a recovery of weeks to months, so timelines posted online are the poster's intentions rather than clinical schedules.[4]

The thread title appears in dozens of posts on looksmax.org going back several years, with variants such as "ascension plan at 17yrs old 511" or "ascension plan with questions high iq help needed", indicating a long-running convention rather than a single viral post.[6][7][8] Wikipedia describes looksmaxxing as an online self-improvement practice divided into softmaxxing (skincare, grooming, fitness) and hardmaxxing (steroids, peptides, surgery), and ascension plans typically span both.[5]

angle.text: The thread itself is a planning tool: it organises changes that do affect appearance (skin, leanness, orthodontics, surgery) into an order, with deadlines and feedback. Members use it to keep a long project in view and to check ideas with others before committing.

paras: Ascension plan threads are titled simply "ascension plan", sometimes with a date range such as "Now-2027" or an age.[1][2] They normally open with the poster's age, height, photos and a list of features they consider weak, written in forum slang ("failos" for flaws).[1]

Content ranges widely. One poster aged 14 listed double-eyelid surgery the following year, a possible Le Fort I or bimaxillary jaw surgery at 18, and later rhinoplasty, alongside ongoing skin treatment, and noted that he expected to grow further.[1] Another laid out phased work on height and facial skeleton, including booking a consultation with an orthognathic surgeon, requesting 3D scans, checking whether pre-surgical orthodontics was needed, arranging sleep and doctor referrals, and planning to involve family and insurance.[2] A third was mostly a body-composition and training schedule: a holiday, a gradual deficit to about 12 percent body fat, whole foods such as liver, beef and eggs, six gym sessions a week, and a hormone cycle planned only after reaching the target leanness.[3]

Staged self-improvement plans predate the term. Wikipedia traces looksmaxxing to incel message boards in the 2010s and the 'PSL' rating forums (PUAHate, Sluthate, Lookism.net), with the term reaching TikTok in the early 2020s.[5] The word 'ascension' is community slang for becoming more attractive, and the 'ascension plan' thread is its planning format on looksmax.org, where title-matching threads appear across many years.[6][7][8]

A 2026 commentary in the Journal of Adolescent Health by Ganson, Piatkowski and Nagata describes looksmaxxing as an online trend of maximising attractiveness, with ordinary practices such as skincare and exercise alongside riskier ones such as steroids, peptides and cosmetic procedures, and notes that its audience trusts influencers, before-and-after images and anecdotes.[9]

Most plans move from low-cost, reversible changes toward expensive or irreversible ones: skin, leanness and grooming first, then dental or skeletal work, then smaller surgeries. Posters attach dates to phases and note financing, such as saving from a job or relying on insurance.[1][2]

Orthognathic surgery, the most common anchor of the larger plans, is jaw surgery to correct skeletal and bite problems. Wikipedia describes it as involving a surgeon and orthodontist working together, pre-surgical orthodontics that has traditionally taken up to a year, initial healing of two to six weeks with bone union taking a further two to four months, and risks including infection (reported up to 7 percent) and nerve numbness that usually recovers within about three months.[4]
Because orthodontic and surgical timing is set by the treating team, posted dates are intentions. Posters also state a fallback, for example growing taller before deciding on surgery.[1][4]

Replies range from encouragement and requests for before-and-after photos to blunt criticism of the plan or the poster. Some replies question whether a poster's timetable is realistic or comment on the forum's culture.[1][2][3] Because the audience is anonymous peers, the feedback is opinion rather than clinical advice. Posters sometimes answer critics by listing their grades, savings or career plans, showing that the thread doubles as a way to present oneself to the community.[1][3]

The Journal of Adolescent Health commentary advises clinicians to ask young people about appearance concerns and body-change behaviours, to separate developmentally typical behaviour from distress, obsessive checking or impaired functioning, to screen for body dysmorphic disorder, eating disorders and substance use, and to take a harm-reduction rather than dismissive approach.[9]

The Cleveland Clinic similarly describes the self-scrutiny encouraged by the culture as able to contribute to body dysmorphic disorder in extreme cases and advises parents to respond with interest rather than judgement.[10]
No studies found of ascension plan threads. Related research covers orthognathic surgery outcomes and, in a 2026 commentary, the health risks of looksmaxxing for boys and young men.[4][9]

timeline.event: Looksmaxxing terminology emerges on incel and PSL rating forums.[5]
Multi-phase 'ascension plan' threads on looksmax.org include planned orthognathic surgery consultations.[1][2]
Journal of Adolescent Health commentary urges clinicians to ask about looksmaxxing behaviours.[9]

lore.intro: Ascension plans are among the most common self-organisation posts on looksmax.org, where members treat a written, phased plan as a way to stay committed and to gather critique.[1][2]

claims.claim: Writing a phased plan with dates makes ascension more achievable
claims.believers: Posters present full plans as a commitment device and expect to report progress with before-and-after photos.[2]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined forum planning threads; surgical timelines are set by clinicians, with recovery commonly spanning weeks to months.[4]

claims.claim: Peer feedback on a plan improves its quality
claims.believers: Posters ask what to add or change, and repliers offer suggestions on order, surgeons and goals.[2][3]
claims.experts: Medical references describe jaw surgery planning as a multidisciplinary clinical process involving surgeons and orthodontists.[4]

claims.claim: Skeletal surgery in the late teens can reset facial structure
claims.believers: A teenage poster plans a jaw procedure at 18 after saving from work, with rhinoplasty later.[1]
claims.experts: Orthognathic surgery is an established treatment for jaw and bite discrepancies, with documented risks such as infection and temporary numbness.[4]

claims.claim: Skin and body composition first creates the best base
claims.believers: Plans lead with skincare and fat loss before surgery.[1][3]
claims.experts: No studies of this ordering were located; clinicians advise screening for body dysmorphic disorder when appearance concern is intense.[9]

claims.claim: Hormone cycles belong in an ascension plan
claims.believers: One plan schedules a growth-focused cycle after reaching a target body-fat level.[3]
claims.experts: The 2026 commentary names steroid and peptide use as higher-risk practices and recommends screening for them in boys and young men.[9]
